mappings.note: Explain 'Lanka padtal shatdal...' -- India imagined as a goddess whose feet the sea washes. The personification-of-nature outcome C-4.2-LO-6. NOTE: duplicated as the next item.
Duplicate of the previous item, with its answer attached. Same mapping.
Which feeling the poem expresses -- the pratipadya of the poem, C-1.1-LO-34.
How India's natural beauty is drawn, and is conserving nature also patriotism: C-1.1-LO-35 for the Bharat-vandana lines, C-2.1 for the opinion the second half asks for.
The word 'shasya'/'upaj' across Eighth Schedule languages -- C-3.2-LO-4 names 'shasya' and its widening of sense outright; CG-4 for the multilingual diversity the list shows.

Who wrote the poem. The poet-introduction outcome C-1.1-LO-33. NOTE: that outcome is worded for Jaishankar Prasad, but this poem and every question here are Nirala's -- a curriculum-side error, reported not fixed.
Nirala's birthplace -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
Where he originally belonged -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
How far his formal schooling went -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
Which languages he taught himself -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
His chief collections of verse -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
He was the first Chhayavadi to use mukt chhand: C-4.3-LO-21 names free verse, C-4.2-LO-5 the Chhayavad it belongs to.
What 'kanak-shasya-kamaldhare' points to in the land -- the Bharat-vandana lines, C-1.1-LO-35.
Why the Himalaya is called India's crown -- nature personified as the goddess's ornament, C-4.2-LO-6.

Find lines for each listed feature: LO-6 for the personification of nature, C-4.3-LO-20 for the alankars, C-3.2-LO-3 for the Sanskritic diction. The samasik-pad row is the one part C-4.3-LO-21 would also cover.
Build a presentation or collage on India's cultural diversity. C-4.2 at competency level and CG-4: the chapter's C-4.2 LOs are Chhayavad and personification, neither of which this is.
Imagine India as a person and dress it in your state's costume and emblems: C-4.2-LO-6 for the personification it extends, C-2.2 for the creative work.
Design a stamp or cover for India and justify the symbols: C-2.2 for the making, C-1.1-LO-35 for the vandana imagery drawn on.
Write a travel account of the Ganga from source to sea -- extended composition, C-2.2.
Gather and weigh the laws made to protect forests -- a reasoned view on a public issue, C-2.1.
How you would present India today: C-2.1 for the argued choice, C-1.1-LO-35 for the poem's own praise of the land it is set against.
How 'shatmukh-shatrav-mukhare' realises 'Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat' -- the vandana of India's many voices, C-1.1-LO-35.
Write a short piece on India's nature, culture and knowledge tradition: C-2.2 for the writing, C-1.1-LO-35 for the poem's terms it draws on.
How pollution and climate change have told on our rivers and the Himalaya -- reasoned view on a current issue, C-2.1.
In how many volumes 'Nirala Rachnavali' appeared -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
With whom his poetry sympathises -- the neglected and the afflicted; poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
The year of his death -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
Whom 'Bharati' stands for -- Bharat Mata and Saraswati together; the vandana, C-1.1-LO-35.
What 'kanak-shasya-kamaldhare' conveys -- the beauty of India's farming tradition, C-1.1-LO-35.
The sense of the same line -- India's plenty of grain and gold, C-1.1-LO-35.
The meaning of 'kanak' -- word sense from the poem's Sanskritic stock, C-3.2-LO-4.
The meaning of 'shasya' -- C-3.2-LO-4 names this very word.
The meaning of 'shatdal' -- C-3.2-LO-4.
What the Lanka-and-sea lines convey -- the land personified with the ocean at her feet, C-4.2-LO-6.
The meaning of 'stav' -- C-3.2-LO-4.
Fill in 'charan yugal' -- recognising the poem's Sanskritic diction, C-3.2-LO-3; the bare word-meaning items are mapped to C-3.2-LO-4.
The meaning of 'vasan' -- C-3.2-LO-4.
Statements on the poem: India's geography personified, Ganga as necklace, Himalaya as crown. C-4.2-LO-6.
What the poem chiefly does -- praises India's knowledge, nature and plenty. The pratipadya, C-1.1-LO-34.
The poem's language and style -- Sanskritic and compound-laden. C-3.2-LO-3.
Assertion-reason: India seen as a conscious being, its quarters ringing with Omkar. Personification, C-4.2-LO-6.
The meaning of 'yugal' -- C-3.2-LO-4.
The meaning of 'khachit' -- C-3.2-LO-4.
Statements about Nirala's temper and works -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
The meaning of 'tushar' -- C-3.2-LO-4.
Which closing line holds the whole poem's central sense -- the pratipadya, C-1.1-LO-34.
Which feeling saturates the poem -- patriotism and inspiration. C-1.1-LO-34.
When and where Nirala was born -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
His schooling and how he gained other languages -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
Name four of his collections -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
In how many volumes and under what name his works appeared -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
His particular contribution in free verse among the Chhayavadis: C-4.3-LO-21 for mukt chhand, C-4.2-LO-5 for the Chhayavad features.
Which class of society his poetry feels for -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
What the poet asks of the land at the poem's opening -- the vandana, C-1.1-LO-35.
Why he addresses her as 'kanak-shasya-kamaldhare' -- C-1.1-LO-35.
The poem's governing feeling and what that epithet brings out: LO-34 for the pratipadya, LO-35 for the line-by-line vandana.
Lanka and the roaring sea figured at the mother's feet: C-4.2-LO-6 for the personification, C-4.3-LO-20 for the roopak that carries it.
Trees, grass and creepers presented as the mother's garments -- personification of nature, C-4.2-LO-6.
Himalaya, Ganga and the Omkar establishing India as a conscious being -- C-4.2-LO-6.
Lanka and the sea shown as servants at her feet -- C-4.2-LO-6.
Explain the sense of 'taru-trin-van-lata vasan, anchal mein khachit suman' -- the vandana lines themselves, C-1.1-LO-35; the how-it-is-presented version of the same lines is mapped to C-4.2-LO-6.
Ganga's white current imagined as the mother's necklace -- C-4.2-LO-6.
The Himalaya's importance from 'mukut shubhra him-tushar' -- the vandana, C-1.1-LO-35.
The spiritual message of 'praan pranav Omkar, dhwanit dishaayen udaar' -- C-1.1-LO-35.
How 'shatmukh-shatrav-mukhare' shows India's variety of thought -- C-1.1-LO-35.
Nirala's life, schooling, languages and literary standing -- poet introduction, C-1.1-LO-33.
His philosophy, prosody and sympathies discussed at length: LO-33 for the poet, C-4.2-LO-5 for the Chhayavad, C-4.3-LO-21 for the free verse.
